power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Do open-text responses add predictive signal beyond structured questionnaire items? A pre-registered test of LLM-derived text features in the DAWBA depression section
table.research_questions:
Hypothesis 1 (directional): Open-text responses carry signal in predicting depression impact incremental to what is found in structured questionnaire responses. This hypothesis, tested separately in each of adolescent- and parent- response cohorts, can be represented more formally as:

    H_A: Δ(R²_full, R²_reduced) > 0
    H_0: Δ(R²_full, R²_reduced) ≤ 0

where ∆(x, y) represents the difference  x-y, R²_full is the test-set R² (coefficient of determination) of some full model including T, and R²_reduced represents the test-set R² of some reduced model excluding T. Three full/reduced pairs will be evaluated: (ST,  S), (QT,  Q), and (SQT, SQ), with a single p-value for each pair derived via non-parametric 1000-iteration permutation shuffling using the Westfall–Young step-down max-T procedure, for each of adolescent- and parent-response cohorts. In this way, hypothesis 1A will test incremental test signal in the adolescent-reported cohort, whereas hypothesis 1B will separately test that in the parent-reported cohort.

Hypothesis 2 (directional): The incremental signal of open-text responses, in supplement of sum scores, exceeds that of granular structured questionnaire responses. This hypothesis can be represented more formally as:

    H_A: Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ) > 0
    H_0: Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ) ≤ 0

where ∆(x, y) represents the difference  x-y, and R²_ST and R²_SQ represent the test-set R² of the stacked ST and SQ regressor models, respectively. A single p-value will be derived via non-parametric 1000-iteration permutation prediction-swapping for each of adolescent- and parent-response cohorts. Similar to Hypothesis 1, Hypothesis 2A will refer to a separate test of the adolescent cohort, whereas Hypothesis 2B will do the same in the parent cohort, separately. 

Estimated effect sizes: 1000-iteration paired bootstrapping will be used to generate 95% CIs for each of  ∆(R²_ST, R²_S), ∆(R²_QT, R²_Q), ∆(R²_SQT, R²_SQ), ∆(R²_ST, R²_SQ) , in each of the adolescent- and parent-report cohorts. Optimistic effect size estimates, given repeat-aggregated R² scores (described in the Indices section) of selected model configurations from exploratory analyses are:

table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin:
Responses to the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) were collected from adolescent participants (age 11-17) and their parents between Summer 2017 and Spring 2021 from the National Institute of Mental Health Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression (CAT-D) study (NIH IRB protocol number 18-M-0037, registered on clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03388606).
The present work is a secondary analysis of that existing dataset, considering 348 paired adolescent- and parent- reported entries. Before any exploration, and after only global cleaning steps requiring no analytic judgment, the data were randomly split 67/33 into development and held-out test sets, stratified by eligibility group. Global cleaning consisted of dropping a single duplicate entry, removing 20 records indicating withdrawal of consent, and subsetting features to only include relevant meta-data and the 84 features of the depression section of the DAWBA, 42 pertaining to each of adolescent and parent responses.

There were 3 participant meta-data features (ID, eligibility, health status) shared across each adolescent-parent participant pair and the 42 depression features were made up of 27 questionnaire responses (with choices {0,1} or {0,1,2}), 10 open-text responses, and 5 depression impact responses (with choices {0,1,2,3}), recorded separately for adolescent and parent responses. No other procedures were applied to the dataset before splitting.

All subsequent processing decisions, model development, hyper-parameter selection, and exploratory analyses were conducted exclusively on the development set. The held-out test set has not been opened, summarized, or analyzed by the research team: no summary statistics, distributions, or outcomes from the test set have been observed. Cleaning rules and model configurations defined on the development set are frozen as of this registration and will be applied to the test set without modification.

table.study_design_overview: This is a secondary analysis of cross-sectional observational data (the depression section of the Development and Well-Being Assessment, DAWBA), with a within-subjects analytic design: competing regression models are trained on a fixed development set and evaluated on the same held-out test participants, so all model comparisons are paired at the participant level. The compared models are defined by their feature sets — a questionnaire sum score (S), granular questionnaire responses (Q), LLM-derived open-text features (T), and their stacked combinations (SQ, ST, QT, SQT). Hypothesis 1 compares three full/reduced pairs (ST vs. S; QT vs. Q; SQT vs. SQ); Hypothesis 2 compares two supplement types on a common base (ST vs. SQ). The entire analysis is replicated separately in two response-cohorts (adolescent self- and parent-report), which constitute separate respondent perspectives on paired participants; the cohorts are analyzed and reported separately rather than compared. All model configurations are selected and frozen using the development set only; the confirmatory analysis will use a single pre-existing development/test split (67/33, stratified by eligibility group) with no test-set access prior to registration.
table.randomization:
This is an observational study with no randomized treatment assignment. Randomization enters at three points: data splitting, cross-validation, and permutation-based inference.
1) Data splitting: Participants were split randomly (67/33) into development and held-out test sets with a random seed (424242), stratified by eligibility group (included or excluded for the study in which the data were originally collected).

2) Cross validation (CV): Exploratory 10-repeated 3-fold CV in the development set used the same eligibility stratification, with an incremental random seed for each repeat (424242, 424243, and so on through 424251).

3) Permutation-based inference: All permutation-based significance testing will use NumPy's random number generator with an incremental random seed for each of the 1000 iterations. This is described further in the Analysis Plan section.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Samples were originally collected between Summer 2017 and Spring 2021 for a broader longitudinal study: the National Institute of Mental Health Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression (CAT-D) study (NIH IRB protocol number 18-M-0037, registered on clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03388606). Participants were asked to respond to the DAWBA, with a financial incentive of $30, in addition to completing a number of other tasks. Recorded eligibility groups at the time of DAWBA completion included:

- Removed from analyses
----Did not or withdrew assent/consent

- Mapped to “excluded”
----Excluded: meets exclusionary criteria (substance use, psychosis, etc.)
----Excluded: does not meet criteria

- Mapped to “included”
----Excluded: cannot be reached or scheduled, all contact options exhausted
----Include: can't scan (braces, etc.)
----Include
----On hold: contact again after specified amount of time
----On hold: low priority

All subsequent processing was conducted separately for parent and adolescent responses, only in the development/exploratory set. Participants marked as excluded due to withdrawing consent were removed from the sample. Additionally, participants not prompted to answer open-response text questions were also removed, serving to limit missing entries and prevent optimistic 0-inflated scores from healthy participants. Participants with any non-structurally missing questionnaire responses or ≥ 6 missing text responses were also removed. The same filtering will be performed on the held-out test set.
table.sample_size: The data is part of a previous longitudinal study collected from Summer 2017 to Spring 2021: the National Institute of Mental Health Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression (CAT-D) study (NIH IRB protocol number 18-M-0037, registered on clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03388606). The subset of data collected used in this study is observational and has already been collected. This raw dataset consists of 348 records, each with paired adolescent-parent responses. One duplicate record was removed. Additionally, participants who withdrew consent were removed, resulting in 327 paired records. Once split, the development and test sets consist of 219 and 108 paired responses, respectively. After separating into parent/adolescent cohorts and removing records based on missing criteria in the development set, the development parent and adolescent cohorts contain n=71 and n=103 participant responses, respectively. Because these cleaned sets originated from a subset of 67% of the full dataset, we anticipate approximately 35 participants in the final parent testing cohort and 50 in the adolescent testing cohort after cleaning.

table.indices:
The modeling framework described in the Measured Variables section is designed as a proxy for the ability of a set of factors to capture contributors/indicators to realized depression impact. The incremental predictive validity of a given factor layer (one of S, Q, T) is represented by how well regression models are able to explain variance in depression impact, given a difference of performance between models with and without that layer. The coefficient of determination (R²) is utilized as a primary performance metric because it measures explanatory power, that is, how much of the variance in reported depression impact is explained by a given model. This is more relevant here than others such as MSE, RMSE, and MAE because it allows for an interpretable measure of how well realized depression is captured by a model compared to a simple guess of the mean, as opposed to a raw measure of error in the model.

Because of limited dataset size, a stratified 10-repeated 3-fold cross-validation (CV) approach was utilized in the development set to explore and select final configurations. This CV framework employed a unique random seed for each of 10 repeats to split data into 3 subsets, stratified again by eligibility group. The designated metric for base evaluation of model performance was repeat-aggregated R² score, which is calculated by concatenating out-of-fold (OOF) predictions across the 3 folds within each repeat, calculating the R² within each repeat, then taking the average over the 10 resulting R² scores. This metric differs slightly from repeat-fold-aggregated R² score, which calculates R² for each set of OOF predictions, averaging over a total of 30 scores. Repeat-aggregated R² score was chosen as the base exploratory metric because it is subject to lower variance, whereas repeat-fold-aggregated R² score was used for formal exploratory model comparison because it allows for insight at a more granular scale.

In the confirmatory analysis, because only a single train-test split will be employed, the metric of interest will simply be the R² score of test-set predictions. Effect size certainty will be quantified via 1000-iteration bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals.
table.statistical_tests:
For convenience, the following description is also attached as a pdf with formatted equations. 

Hypotheses 1A/1B: Open-text responses carry signal in predicting depression impact incremental to what is found in structured questionnaire responses. This hypothesis can be represented more formally as:

    H_A: Δ(R²_full, R²_reduced) > 0
    H_0: Δ(R²_full, R²_reduced) ≤ 0

where Δ(x, y) represents the difference x − y, R²_full is the test-set R² of some full model including T, and R²_reduced represents the test-set R² of some reduced model excluding T. Three full/reduced pairs will be evaluated: (ST, S), (QT, Q), and (SQT, SQ).

The null hypothesis states that T carries no predictive information, meaning that a model including T performs no better than the same model without it. To construct this null, a permutation procedure will destroy the link between each participant and their text-derived vector while leaving all other data intact. For each of 1000 iterations, a unique random seed will be used to shuffle the text-derived vectors among participants in the train set, stratified by eligibility group, such that a participant only receives the vector of another participant within the same eligibility group. Within each iteration, the same shuffled train set participants are used for all three full models: each of ST, QT, SQT is refit on the shuffled train set and evaluated on the un-shuffled test set, yielding a null R² for each. The reduced models (S, Q, SQ) contain no text features and are therefore unaffected by the shuffle; their observed test-set R² values are held fixed across iterations, so each iteration yields three null differences Δ(R²_ST, R²_S), Δ(R²_QT, R²_Q), and Δ(R²_SQT, R²_SQ).

Because T should demonstrate incremental value regardless of which structured-response baseline it supplements, the three pairwise differences are treated as a family of hypotheses, with family-wise error rate (FWER) controlled at α = 0.05 using the Westfall-Young step-down max-T procedure.

Let the observed differences be the set d = {d₁, d₂, d₃}, where

    d₁ = Δ(R²_ST,  R²_S)
    d₂ = Δ(R²_QT,  R²_Q)
    d₃ = Δ(R²_SQT, R²_SQ)

and let d_ji denote the corresponding null difference from permutation iteration i for hypothesis j. The observed differences are ordered from largest to smallest, d₍₁₎ ≥ d₍₂₎ ≥ d₍₃₎, where d₍k₎ denotes the k-th largest observed difference in d. Adjusted p-values are computed step-down. The null statistic for step k = 1 in permutation iteration i is m₍₁₎i = max_j d_ji across all three permuted differences. The corresponding hypothesis of d₍₁₎ is then removed from consideration for further testing. Accordingly, for step k = 2 in permutation iteration i, m₍₂₎i is the maximum across the two remaining hypotheses {d₍₂₎i, d₍₃₎i}, and m₍₃₎i is simply the single remaining permuted difference d₍₃₎i. The raw adjusted p-value for the k-th ordered hypothesis is

                1 + Σ(i = 1 to 1000) 1[ m₍k₎i ≥ d₍k₎ ]
    p̃₍k₎  =  ──────────────────
                             1000 + 1

after which monotonicity is enforced by taking successive maxima across all p-values, p₍k₎ = max(p̃₍₁₎, …, p̃₍k₎). Because all three null differences within an iteration are computed from a single shared shuffle, the permutation distribution preserves the dependence among the hypotheses, so the procedure adapts to their correlation rather than assuming independence, serving to increase power over conservative alternative FWER controls such as the Bonferroni correction. A hypothesis is rejected if its adjusted p-value falls below α = 0.05. 1000-iteration paired bootstrapping will be used to generate 95% CIs for each of Δ(R²_ST, R²_S), Δ(R²_QT, R²_Q), and Δ(R²_SQT, R²_SQ).


Hypotheses 2A/2B: The incremental signal of open-text responses, in supplement of sum scores, exceeds that of granular structured questionnaire responses. This question can be represented more formally as:

    H_A: Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ) > 0
    H_0: Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ) ≤ 0

where Δ(x, y) represents the difference x − y, and R²_ST and R²_SQ represent the test-set R² of the stacked ST and SQ regressor models, respectively. A one-sided test is pre-specified based on the direction indicated by Bayesian post-hoc comparisons in the development set during exploratory analyses. Unlike Hypothesis 1, the null hypothesis here does not assert that T carries no information. Under H_0, both T and Q may carry signal, and the claim is only that ST does not outperform SQ, meaning a train-set shuffle would therefore construct the wrong null. Instead, a per-participant prediction-swap (sign-flip) procedure will be employed, under which the null of exchangeability states that the assignment of the labels "ST" and "SQ" to each participant's pair of predictions is arbitrary.

The frozen ST and SQ configurations will each be trained once on the full development set, producing a pair of test-set predictions (ŷ_ST,i , ŷ_SQ,i) for each of the n test participants. The observed statistic is computed on these baseline predictions as t_obs = Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ). For each of 1000 iterations, a unique random seed will be used to swap ŷ_ST,i and ŷ_SQ,i independently for each participant i with probability 0.5. Both R² values are then recomputed on the swapped prediction vectors and their difference recorded as t_i. Note that models are trained only once, as permutation applies exclusively to test-set predictions. This contrasts with the Hypothesis 1 procedure, which retrains models under each train-set shuffle. Significance will once again be set at α = 0.05, and p-value defined as:

               1 + Σ(i = 1 to 1000) 1[ t_i ≥ t_obs ]
    p  =  ──────────────────
                            1000 + 1

1000-iteration bootstrapping will also be utilized to generate a 95% CI of Δ(R²_ST, R²_SQ).
table.transformations: Participant autobiographical text will be transformed into 80-dimensional feature vectors representing the presence/intensity of a taxonomy of 80 psychological outcomes. This is described in the measured variables section.
table.inference_criteria:
Specific testing procedures for hypotheses are described in further detail in the Statistical models section. This section provides further detail into inference criteria.

Hypothesis 1A and 1B will test text's incremental explanatory value to structured questionnaire responses in adolescent- and parent-reported DAWBA responses, respectively, in relation to reported depression impact scores. For each of the two hypotheses, 3 p-values will be obtained: one pertaining to each of ∆(R²_ST, R²_S), ∆(R²_QT, R²_Q), ∆(R²_SQT, R²_SQ). These tests are not independent, so a Westfall-Young step-down max-T procedure will be employed to control the FWER at α = 0.05, and monotonicity will be enforced such that p_k = max(p̃_1, …, p̃_k) for each pair's p-value. Thus, a rejection of any single pair constitutes evidence against the global null that T carries no incremental signal. Hypothesis 1 will therefore be supported in a given cohort if at least one of the three adjusted p-values meets the standard p < 0.05 threshold. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals will be derived for each pair in each cohort, regardless of significance.

Hypothesis 2A and 2B will test text's incremental explanatory power over sum scores' superiority to that of granular questionnaire responses in adolescent- and parent-reported DAWBA responses, respectively, in relation to reported depression impact scores. A single p-value for each of 2A and 2B will be calculated, with significance once again set at the standard p < 0.05.

Hypothesis 1 and 2 each have a pair of A/B tests associated with them, each evaluated separately in adolescent- and parent-report cohorts. Although not statistically independent, since there exists overlap in paired responses, each addresses a distinct respondent perspective and constitutes a separate claim. All four results will be reported in full, and no conclusion will be extended from one of the four tests to another. Accordingly, no correction will be applied across cohorts (A/B) or hypothesis classes (Hypothesis 1/2).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants who withdrew consent for the study in which the data was originally collected have already been excluded from all analyses (exploratory and prospective confirmatory). The following exclusion criteria in exploratory analyses will be applied to participants in the held-out test set for confirmatory analyses:

- At least 1 non-systematic missing questionnaire response
- 6 or more missing text 
----Includes not being prompted to respond to open-text questions

Because questionnaire and impact data were collected on rigid scales, and numerical text representation extraction is constrained to a vector whose values are on a rigid scale, there are inherently no outliers to detect and/or remove.
table.missing_data_handling: The DAWBA framework conditions prompting participants to respond to certain sections based on responses to previous sections. As such, participants not prompted to answer open-text questions will be removed. Missing values for questionnaire responses in the case of not being prompted will simply be marked as 0.  For all other cases of missing entries in questionnaire responses, the whole participant will be dropped. Participants with 6 or more missing entries for text responses will be dropped and answers are filled as “Not answered” for participants with 5 or less missing entries. The described framework of dealing with incomplete or missing data in the held-out test set is in line with what was performed on the train set during exploratory analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
In addition to assessing the incremental signal of T, and how it compares to that of Q in supplement of S, the contributions of individual components of T are also of interest. This planned exploratory analysis in the test set is supported by a number of methods employed in the development set. Note that all completed preliminary and planned future analyses were performed separately for adolescent and parent cohorts.

Given final selected model configurations, an exploratory analysis of feature contributions will be performed for indication of how each feature affects model output in practice, using the test set. Explored in two dimensions, the salience of features and incremental R² provide a holistic view of each feature's effect on both raw output and aggregated performance. Because the SQT set-up explained the most variance (via development repeat-aggregated R²) in both adolescent and parent cohorts, this is the only stacked framework in which contribution was, and will be, analyzed.

To gain insight into how, on average, the values of features push predictions up/down, a salience analysis was performed in the development set. Given a frozen residual regressor model trained on the development set, recorded feature values in the development set were multiplied by the learned weights of corresponding features in the model. Values across records for each feature were aggregated across minimum, maximum, average, and standard deviation. The same procedure will be performed in the held-out test set, where learned weights from frozen SQT models will be multiplied by corresponding feature values in the held-out test set. These values have the ability to uncover that a feature with a relatively low/high weight magnitude is counterintuitively affecting model output by a large/small magnitude, given the distribution of recorded values for a given feature. Additionally, the results of the salience mapping in the development and held-out test sets will be compared for insight into feature consistencies across the two sets.

A salience analysis provides insight into model behavior given feature values, but an analysis of behavior given the target variable provides insight into how informative or degradative the learned signal from a feature is, providing a more holistic heuristic of desirable feature contribution. The Lindeman, Merenda, and Gold method, also known as LMG decomposition, apportions variance explained among individual predictors by recording incremental variance explained given the presence/absence of a feature. Because the incremental R² of a feature may differ depending on the pre-existing feature set, the process of adding a given feature and recording incremental performance must be repeated many times with many different pre-existing feature sets.

Because T enters the stacked framework as its final layer, the decomposition is applied to the T layer alone: every ordering begins from the fitted SQ prediction, so the recorded increments apportion the incremental variance explained by the text vector over and above sum score and structured responses, rather than the total variance explained by the SQT model. The S and Q layers are not apportioned. The 80 text-feature contributions therefore sum to ∆(R²_SQT, R²_SQ) for a given iteration of LMG. Note that this total is invariant to the ordering in which features are added; only its allocation across features depends on the ordering. Two distinct implementations were preliminarily explored in the development set.

**Single-split Implementation** The first, and the simpler of the two, used the same exploratory dataset that final models were trained on as an ad-hoc evaluation set. For a single final trained model, 500 random feature orderings of the 80-text derived features were generated, each from a unique random seed, and each was evaluated alongside its reverse, for 1000 orderings in total. The process of iteratively adding features and recording evaluation-set performance was carried out for every one of the 1000 orderings, and each text feature's incremental variance explained was averaged to give a single contribution value per feature. This method is heavily biased, since it is simply a measure of how much each feature helps the model memorize the training data.

**CV Implementation** The second implementation addressed this limitation by embedding LMG within the same stratified 10-repeated 3-fold CV framework employed to select final model configurations. Here, 1000 random feature orderings were generated, each from a unique random seed, and each was again evaluated alongside its reverse, for 2000 orderings in total. A given ordering was evaluated in all 30 (repeat, fold) cells of the CV framework: within a cell, the model was fit on the two training folds and features were added iteratively, with the incremental OOF R² recorded at each addition. Each feature's final contribution was the mean of its increment across all 1000 × 2 × 30 = 60,000 (ordering, direction, cell) evaluations. Unlike the first implementation, contributions were estimated out of fold, so a feature whose learned signal does not generalize received a low or negative average contribution.

A secondary exploratory analysis will be performed in the held-out test set. This exploration will employ the single-split implementation of LMG on the held-out test set over 1000 iterations and their reversals, for a total of 2000. Since the frozen models are not trained on the held-out test set, LMG results via the single-split method will provide an unbiased estimate of each feature's unique predictive power. These results will be compared to those of the CV Implementation in the development set, providing insight into the consistency of individual contributions.

Additionally, exploratory sensitivity analyses will be performed for insight into any potential biases or unforeseen relationships between test-set performance and aspects of the data. For example, we will look at the pairwise relationship between performance and sex, missingness, and/or date of questionnaire completion. An analysis on the characteristics of excluded participant records will also be performed to uncover potential biases caused by our filtering framework. Further, a comparison of single-layer S, Q, and T model test-set performance will be performed, as there was no clear trend in predictive ability across adolescent and parent cohorts in the development set.

ownership.dep_description: Structured questionnaires are an established method for depression screening in adolescents. However, they may be limited in their ability to capture a sufficient account of an adolescent's experience. Open-text responses, collected alongside structured items, allow adolescents and parents to describe their interpretation of experiences more freely and may capture more nuanced information. text.text: Depression in adolescents has grown in prevalence in the past decade.
Despite indications of differences in symptom presentation, measurement properties, and treatment response between adolescents and adults, research is dominated by adult participants.

Qualitative work has identified symptomatic and functional domains important to depressed adolescents and those around them; however, there remains little quantitative evidence of how these domains relate to the functional impact of the disorder.

In this preregistered study, we use adolescent self-report (n = 153) and parent-report (n = 106) responses in the depression section of the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) to examine what information relevant to reported depression impact may be missing from its structured symptom-scale.
We apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to participant free-text answers to extract information on a taxonomy of 80 outcomes.

Through a sequential residual stacking framework that estimates incremental information in symptom sum-scores (S ), item-level symptom-scale answers (Q), and LLM-derived text representations (T ), we find that parent text contains information relevant to their report of depression impact that is not available in the structured symptom-scale, with the largest contributions concentrated in functioning-related domains (e.g., professional responsibilities, social exclusion, autonomy, coping).
No such evidence was found in adolescent self-reports.
Given the moderate sample size, these results are preliminary.

Nonetheless, we provide a proof-of-concept framework for extracting information from open-ended free text in large existing datasets, and estimating incremental information across sources, which could be applied to uncover specific aspects of adolescent mental disorders across populations.

Indicators of poor mental health among adolescents have risen in the past decades.

In the United States, rates of major depressive episodes among adolescents increased by 52% (8.7% to 13.2%) from 2005-2017 (Twenge, Cooper, Joiner, Duffy, & Binau, 2019), and persistent sadness or hopelessness among U.S. high school students rose from 30% in 2013 to a peak of 42% in 2021 before falling to 40% in 2023 (Verlenden et al., 2024).

text.text: However, the majority of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) research has been conducted in adults, despite numerous studies suggesting potential differences in manifestation, latent structure, and response to treatment of the disorder between adolescents and adults (Rice et al., 2019; Wight, Sepúlveda, & Aneshensel, 2004).

text.text: We aim to address this gap directly through perspectives of adolescent experiences.
MDD is an inherently hard phenomenon to measure.

It is heterogeneous and manifests in many different ways, with low overlap in symptoms across individuals (Fried & Nesse, 2015) and moderate overlap across established scales (Fried, 2017 (Fried, , 2020)).

text.text: A systematic review of 138 studies spanning 170 different study populations by Haroz et al. (2017) found that only seven of fifteen frequently mentioned features of depression worldwide are part of the DSM criteria for MDD.

text.text: In response, numerous qualitative studies have been conducted to derive factors relevant to depressed people that may not be captured adequately in standard instruments. Krause, Midgley, Edbrooke-Childs, and Wolpert (2021) conducted a post-hoc qualitative analysis of interview data collected for the IMPACT-ME study (Goodyer et al., 2011; Midgley, Ansaldo, & Target, 2014), with adolescent, parent, and therapist participants.

text.text: A taxonomy of 29 outcome domains most prominently discussed by participants was derived, with very few of them consistently reported in recent quantitative treatment outcome studies.

Similarly, Chevance et al. (2020) surveyed patients reporting a depressive disorder, informal care-givers, and healthcare professionals about their perspectives of the expected benefits of depression treatment.

text.text: From these responses, a taxonomy of 80 outcome domains was derived.

These studies identify what matters to people with depression and those around them, but do not directly quantify how much these additional domains contribute to the impact a disorder has on a person's life.

Testing this quantitatively may be accomplished with: 1) an open description of experiences from participants alongside structured symptom measures, 2) a measure of the impact of depression, and 3) a method for extracting numerical representations of potentially relevant domains from those descriptions.
The Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) provides the first two requirements (R. Goodman, Ford, Richards, Gatward, & Meltzer, 2000).
text.formatted: The Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) provides the first two requirements (R. Goodman, Ford, Richards, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gatward, & Meltzer, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: It features responses from adolescents, their parents and, occasionally, their teachers on a set of questionnaires, impact ratings, and structured free-text interviews for a number of mental-health disorders, including depression.
Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP), specifically in large language models (LLMs), have made the third possible.

For example, Xin et al. (2026) developed logistic regression classifiers operating on text embeddings to classify transcribed interview text as exemplifying a given outcome, after training on human-coded labels (Krause et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Xin et al. (2026)</ref> developed logistic regression classifiers operating on text embeddings to classify transcribed interview text as exemplifying a given outcome, after training on human-coded labels <ref type="bibr">(Krause et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, this framework of training classifiers operating on text embeddings requires large amounts of human-coded data, which may not always be available for the outcomes of interest.
The latest LLMs make a different approach feasible, namely to predict the presence (or absence) of each outcome directly, after reading a prompt defining the outcome and the text to be classified.
In this way, it is possible to efficiently quantify elements of already-collected semi-structured text at a large scale.

In this preregistered study (Matar, Lossio-Ventura, Pereira, & Nielson, 2026), we combine these elements to test whether free text contains information relevant to the impact of depression beyond that which is present in symptom rating scales.
text.formatted: In this preregistered study <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Matar, Lossio-Ventura, Pereira, & Nielson, 2026)</ref>, we combine these elements to test whether free text contains information relevant to the impact of depression beyond that which is present in symptom rating scales.

text.text: Using already-collected depression data from adolescent and parent responses to the DAWBA, we hypothesize that text adds information above symptom rating scale sumscores, item-level symptom ratings, and their combination.
We also hypothesize that supplementing sumscores with information derived from text will be more predictive than when supplementing with individual symptom ratings.
We test this with a residual stacking framework that allows for the isolation of contributed signal to specific sources, and additionally attribute added signal to specific outcome domains.

In testing our hypotheses, we also demonstrate an analytical framework that makes it possible to exploit existing free-text data to discover and assess the importance of previously unmeasured aspects of adolescent mental health disorders across cultures, ages, and/or sex.
All hypotheses were motivated by exploratory analyses in a development set.
Models frozen prior to confirmatory analyses were fit on the development set and evaluated on participants in the held-out set.

text.text: Twenty participant pairs were removed due to withdrawal of consent.
Only participant metadata and responses to the depression section of the DAWBA were considered for our analyses.
Free-text responses were manually de-identified prior to inclusion in this study.
The preprocessed dataset of 327 paired parent-adolescent records was initially split into development (n=219, ∼ 67%) and held-out (n=108, ∼ 33%) sets, stratified by eligibility to the CAT-D study.
The following processing steps were decided upon and performed in the development set, followed by the held-out set after preregistration.
While all of these data were used as part of the screening process for the CAT-D study, we did not access the held-out set for other purposes prior to the execution of the preregistered analyses.
Each adolescent participant is the subject of both a self-report and parent-report response set.
These were separated into two response samples (adolescent and parent), and all subsequent processing and analyses were conducted separately within each.
Exclusion criteria were applied to responses independently, such that excluding an informant's response in one sample did not necessarily remove the matched response in the other sample.
Consequently, the final samples contain partially overlapping, rather than matched, sets of adolescent self-and parent-responses.
Additionally, splitting into development and held-out sets prior to separating the two response samples ensured that there was no overlap of adolescent participants across splits.
Four symptom-scale items (18i-18l, covering ideation and attempt of self-harm/suicide) were largely missing in both samples and thus excluded from analysis.
The DAWBA uses skip logic, prompting informants to complete later sections only on the basis of their earlier answers.
As such, the responses of informants not prompted to answer semi-structured free-text questions were removed.
Missing values for symptom-scale items as a result of not being prompted were simply marked as 0.
For all other cases of missing entries in symptom-scale items, the whole response was removed.
Responses with 6 or more missing text entries were dropped, and any missing answers were filled as "Not answered" for responses with 5 or fewer missing entries.
After all cleaning steps, the adolescent and parent development sets contained 103 and 71 responses, respectively, over 120 unique adolescent participants.
All processing steps described were applied to the adolescent and parent held-out sets as well, resulting in 50 and 35 responses, respectively, over 60 unique adolescent subjects.

The target outcome for prediction is Impact Score, which is taken as the sum of five depression impact questions at the end of the depression section of the DAWBA (shown in Table 12 in the Supplemental Materials).

text.text: This target is predicted within a residual stacking framework, which makes it possible to isolate the incremental signal present in three classes of predictor features.
The first class of features, denoted as S, is the sum of 23 individual items in the depression symptom-scale section of the DAWBA, with a possible discrete range of [0,25].
The second, Q, is a 23-dimensional vector of item-level answers to the symptom-scale section of the questionnaire, with response options of {0,1} or {0,1,2}.
The third class is T, which is an 80-dimensional numerical representation of informant answers to free-text prompts.
The signal of a given class of features is quantified as the out-of-sample coefficient of determination (R² ) of a linear regression predicting Impact Score from the input features chosen.
This metric was selected over others such as MSE, RMSE, or MAE because it provides insight into performance relative to a simple guess of the mean, rather than raw error.
In each sample, S, Q, and T were used to predict Impact Score.
A number of residual stacking setups were explored, including single-layer (S, Q, T ), two-layer (ST, QT, SQ), and three-layer (SQT ) setups.
All S -layer models were simple linear regressions, whereas Q-and T -layers were ridge regressions, regardless of position in a given stacked setup.
Multi-layer setups were implemented such that a given layer's residuals served as the target of the subsequent layer.
For example, in the SQT model, a linear regression was fit on S to predict Impact Score, then a ridge regression model was fit on Q to predict the error of the S model.
This resulted in an SQ model whose final output was the sum of S -model outputs and its predictions of S residuals.
Finally, another ridge regression model was fit on T to predict the error of the SQ model, whose final outputs were the sum of the SQ model and its prediction of the SQ model error.
This framework is outlined in Table 3.

text.text: The difference in R² (variance explained) between S /SQ or SQ/SQT provides insight into incremental signal available in Q or T when they are added.

Furthermore, any shared variance is assigned to the lower level models, so that the difference in out-of-sample R² between SQ and SQT only represents the unique additional variance explained by T. We use the out-of-sample R² because in-sample R² is trivially non-decreasing as features are added, but out-of-sample R² reflects generalized performance and penalizes overfitting.
All the prediction models tested were fit using the entirety of the development set, and out-ofsample prediction results were obtained by deploying them on the held-out set.
The development set was used to select lambda regularization penalties for Q-and T -layers, as well as a number of methods and configurations to derive numerical representations of text.

The first, LR, involved embedding text and using the resulting numeric vectors as inputs to previously trained logistic regression models for each outcome domain, similar to work done by Xin et al. (2026).

text.text: The second, LLM Prompting, involved prompting LLMs to test the presence of the outcome domain in the text directly.
The ultimate goal in both cases was to represent text as a numeric vector reflecting some taxonomy of mental health symptoms/outcomes/domains.
This exploration is described in further detail in the Model Configuration Selection section of the Supplemental Materials.
Ultimately, we chose LLM Prompting as the method of derivation, using the taxonomy of 80 mental health outcomes derived by Chevance et al. (2020).
text.formatted: Ultimately, we chose LLM Prompting as the method of derivation, using the taxonomy of 80 mental health outcomes derived by <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Chevance et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: For this method, the 10 free-text items, including both question and answer, were first concatenated into one large block of text before wrapping in a broader prompt, which gave context to the text and provided instructions for what to output.
LLMs were prompted independently for each outcome in the taxonomy and for each response.
The resulting feature vector for each instance of T was an 80-dimensional concatenation of LLM output.
There were multiple decisions to make regarding the configuration of LLM prompting, which we will refer to as pseudo-hyperparameters.
Namely, these involve the LLM base-model, temperature, prompting method, and output type.
Pseudo-hyperparameters were selected separately for each residual setup including T (T, ST, QT, SQT ) within each response-sample, for a total of eight selected sets of pseudo-hyperparameters.
LLM base-models were selected from Gemini 2.5 Pro, Qwen 3.6 27B and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct.
Qwen and Llama are open-weight models, which we ran on local hardware.
Gemini was run through HHS Enterprise Gemini with FedRAMP High authorization.
These models, developed by different entities, differ in size, capability, and price.
Estimated performance rankings varied across residual setups and response-samples in the development set.
Temperature, a true hyperparameter of LLMs, controls the stochasticity of output.
Smaller temperature settings result in more deterministic and consistent output across runs, but may limit variation in LLM output and ability to capture nuance.
We also considered two different LLM prompting approaches.

In our zero-shot prompting, we provided a description of the source of the text, a concatenated block of DAWBA free-text questions and answers, the target domain, a definition of that domain, and instructions for output.

In contrast, our few-shot prompting supplemented the provided description of the domain with a few examples of text and expected output, providing further information about the intended interpretation of the domain.
An important consideration of few-shot prompting is that, if provided examples are too narrow, LLMs may not be able to generalize or capture more nuanced information as intended.
Similarly, if they are too broad, LLMs may have a wider view of a domain than is appropriate.
Further, all chosen pseudo-hyperparameter sets employed a Scale output type, which prompted LLMs to output the severity ({0,1,2,3,4}) of an outcome.
This is in contrast to the Binary output type, which prompted LLMs to simply output whether the outcome was present in the text or not ({0,1}).
An example of zero-shot, scale prompting is displayed in the Supplemental Materials.
These pseudo-hyperparameters were selected alongside lambda (λ), a true regularization hyperparameter of ridge regression.
Generally, larger values of lambda place higher penalty on learned coefficients and constrain the model fit to the training set, reducing the likelihood of over-fitting.

text.text: The starting point for our work was the availability of the DAWBA instrument, used in the context of depression.
There, adolescents and parents answer a structured questionnaire composed of symptom-scale items (Q), which can be aggregated into sum-scores (S ), as well as providing short free-text narratives.
Using LLMs, the latter can be transformed into quantitative features representing a taxonomy of 80 mental-health outcomes (Chevance et al., 2020) (T ).
Our main objective was to determine if there was information in free text relevant to the impact of depression that was not captured by the structured symptom-scale.
We operationalized this through a residual stacking framework capable of isolating predictive capability of each source in prediction of adolescent-and parent-reported impact of depression.
We hypothesized that T would increase variance explained over S, Q, and stacked SQ models in both adolescent-and parent-response samples.
This was supported in the parent-response sample over Q (∆R² = 0.068, p minP = 0.033) and SQ (∆R² = 0.060, p minP = 0.033), but not S (∆R² = 0.039, p minP = 0.11).
No significant increases from T were found in adolescent responses (∆R² between -0.107 and 0.049, p minP between 0.26 and 0.76).

We additionally hypothesized that the incremental signal of T as a supplement to S would exceed that of Q, but found no significant results in either sample, with near-zero or negative observed differences in performance between ST and SQ (∆R² = -0.027 and -0.004 for adolescent and parent responses, respectively).
Given the limited power of this proof-of-concept study, we did not aim to draw conclusions about the difference between adolescent self-report and parent-report.
While we did observe a difference in significance for Hypothesis 1, we did not test the difference in incremental R² between parents and adolescents.

This difference may partly reflect the longer written answers by parents, whose median free-text word count exceeded that of adolescents by 19 in the held-out set (182 vs 163 words) and 51 in the development set (249 vs 198 words).
It is also possible that there is greater inter-individual consistency between parent free-text responses than there is between adolescent responses.
Our results in the parent-response sample are consistent with semi-structured text containing information about depression impact that is not available in structured symptom-scale items.
Although T alone explained far less variance in parent-reported impact than S or Q alone (0.073 vs.
0.297 and 0.272), its contribution was almost entirely complementary: T increased explained variance by 0.068 over Q and 0.060 over SQ, nearly its full standalone value.
This suggests that the information T carries about parent-reported impact overlaps little with that captured by the symptom-scale items.
This was not the case for S (∆R² = 0.039, p minP = 0.11).
It is noteworthy that the two significant comparisons both used zero-shot Qwen, whereas few-shot Llama was employed for ST.
We selected Llama for the S to ST comparison because of its superior performance in the development set.
In an exploratory sensitivity analysis, ST did explain significantly more variance than S (∆R² = 0.088, p = 0.04) when free-text features were extracted with zero-shot Qwen instead of few-shot Llama.
Thus, the failure to confirm this hypothesis was likely due to noise in the selection of models in the development set.
Given the indication that T contains predictive information disjoint from that in the symptom-scale in parent responses, it is worth exploring the nature of that unique signal.
T was extracted from semistructured text following a taxonomy of 80 domains originally derived from a qualitative study by Chevance et al. (2020).

text.text: These outcomes were segmented into two classes of symptom-(64 total) and functioningrelated (16 total) domains, as psychiatric classifications often distinguish between the two.

Symptom-related domains, pertaining to the manifestations of a disorder, are among the most studied, whereas functioningrelated domains, pertaining to the extent to which those manifestations affect various aspects of daily life, receive less attention (Krause et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Symptom-related domains, pertaining to the manifestations of a disorder, are among the most studied, whereas functioningrelated domains, pertaining to the extent to which those manifestations affect various aspects of daily life, receive less attention <ref type="bibr">(Krause et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The two, which are both typically required for a diagnosis of MDD (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), are related but do not fully overlap.

Functional impairment has been found to be only partially explained by symptom severity and, in children and adolescents, functional impact has been shown to predict later psychiatric disorder over and above baseline symptoms (Stringaris & Goodman, 2013).

text.text: Thus, it is plausible to conclude that consideration of both may provide a better picture of a disorder than either alone.

Because the structured DAWBA items primarily capture symptoms (R. Goodman et al., 2000), remaining relevant information not already captured might therefore be expected to concentrate in functioning-related domains.

text.text: Consistent with this, functioning-related domains were over-represented among the features contributing to T 's increment in the parent QT and SQT models, the only two residual setups where T added significant gains.
Of 18 LLM-derived features, selected as the union of the top 10 contributors across development and held-out sets in each model, eight contributed positively in all four groups.

Five of the eight were functioningrelated domains (Professional responsibilities, Personal development, Social exclusion, Autonomy, Coping with life events), whereas three were symptom-related (Cognitive flexibility, Irritability, Self-confidence), despite functioning domains making up only 16 of the 80 in the taxonomy.
Their prevalence in the original study deriving them (Chevance et al., 2020) is mixed.

text.text: Professional responsibilities (11%) was among the most mentioned by all participants.

Self-confidence (4.2%) was less mentioned, followed by Autonomy (4%), Coping with life events (4%), Irritability (3%), Personal development (1%), Social exclusion (< 1%), and Cognitive flexibility, which was only mentioned in the French cohort (< 1%).

text.text: Suicidal Ideation (symptomrelated, 23%) was the most frequently mentioned domain, but was not determined to be a major contributor when supplementing Q and SQ in our data.

The predominance of functioning-related domains among these contributors may explain the discrepancy between significant results in the two responder samples, as parents tend to focus more on functioning than adolescents (Krause et al., 2021).

text.text: There are two potential interpretations relating to the prevalence of functioning-related domains in the extracted set of top contributors.
The first offers that T recovers clinically meaningful content (the consequences of depression for school, peer, family life, etc.) that symptom-oriented structured items do not elicit.
The second understands T as simply providing a finer-grained description of the outcome itself.

The DAWBA impact score is defined as the sum of five prompts relating to distress and interference in everyday domains such as family life, friendships, and schoolwork, so parent descriptions of social exclusion or difficulties with schoolwork overlap in content with the construct being predicted.
These interpretations are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

A deeper understanding of these results would benefit from further analyses distinguishing between text serving to effectively extend the structured screening and text merely refining the measure of impairment that structured impact items already target.

Outside of the results' implications in depression screenings, this study also serves as a proof-of-concept framework for evaluating the utility and/or nature of semi-structured text in relation to associated structured data, allowing for analysis of already-collected data at large scales in mental health domains.

Previous work has explored similar residual stacking approaches in bioinformatics (Boulesteix & Hothorn, 2010; Boulesteix & Sauerbrei, 2011), and others have employed both feature extraction from social media postings via NLP and residual stacking broadly applied in health, psychology, and economics (Zamani & Schwartz, 2017; Zamani, Schwartz, Lynn, Giorgi, & Balasubramanian, 2018).

text.text: However, to our knowledge, this is the first preregistered test of whether LLM-derived text features add predictive value above structured symptom scale questions in relation to depression impact.

Although our framework is not specific to the DAWBA, the assessment is a particularly well-suited instrument for further investigations, as it was developed to be administered by lay-interviewers (R. Goodman et al., 2000), lowering barriers for administration and making collection more accessible.

text.text: The DAWBA also features various skip rules throughout, making assumptions that a section is unlikely to be relevant given previous responses, and in turn reducing the burden of completion for participants.

In addition to further investigations exploring the questions posed by this study, any number of taxonomies may be used to assess differences in information found in free-text across age, cultural, or sex groups, in prediction of reported impact of depression, or any other mental-health disorder in the DAWBA.

There have already been numerous collections of the DAWBA across cultural (Alyahri & Goodman, 2006; A. Goodman et al., 2012; Zeinoun et al., 2013), age, and sex groups (Baser, Ford, Delgado, O'Logbon, & Cross, 2023).

text.text: A major limitation of this study is the relatively small sample sizes.
In the held-out set, this lowers power and decreases reliability of observed effect sizes, as evidenced by wide CIs.

Model and hyperparameter selection within the development set are also affected by this, given potential variance in results, although comparisons were conducted across aggregated 10-time repeated 3-fold CV scores to minimize the volatility of model performance estimates and rankings.

Additionally, the sample was purposefully filtered to exclude participants not prompted to respond to freetext questions, removing a vast majority of healthy volunteers with 0 impact and avoiding spurious inflation of variance explained.
This, paired with included participants being help-seeking, may have reduced the proportion of explainable variance by increasing the homogeneity of our sample.
This may explain the low magnitude of observed R² , though these values are comparable with similar analyses predicting depression impact from symptoms (Stringaris & Goodman, 2013).
text.formatted: This may explain the low magnitude of observed R² , though these values are comparable with similar analyses predicting depression impact from symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Stringaris & Goodman, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Another potential limitation is that explained variance estimates may be inflated by shared-informant variance (also referred to as shared-rater or shared-method variance), which may produce artifactual covariance between predictors (S, Q, T, and their stacked setups) and reported impact (Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee, & Podsakoff, 2003).

text.text: Because the same respondent provides the symptom-scale ratings, free text, and impact ratings within each sample, variance explained may reflect genuine capture of contributors to impact, but it could also reflect the consistency of a respondent in describing the adolescent's experiences across all three sources.
Cross-informant analyses, such as predicting adolescent-reported impact from parent text, or prediction of clinician-rated outcomes, would help separate these possibilities.
Additionally, statistical corrections may be effective, but likely require larger datasets than available here (Podsakoff et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Additionally, statistical corrections may be effective, but likely require larger datasets than available here <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Podsakoff et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our selected LLMs may not remain accessible for validation in the future.
Gemini is closed-source and the specific version used here may be discontinued later.
Open-weight models were purposefully explored with this in mind, although they present a barrier of their own by requiring access to one or more GPUs to run locally.
This may also be the only option if cloud-based models cannot be used with data containing PHI or PII.
These findings, although preliminary, have implications in our understanding of adolescent depression, specifically in the operationalization of that understanding through screenings.

Significant increases in parentreported impact variance explained with the inclusion of LLM-derived text features over structured item responses suggest that semi-structured interview responses may contain explicit, unique information unavailable in the structured symptom-scale.

This claim would benefit from further testing on larger samples to decrease uncertainty in observed effect sizes, increase efficacy of statistical corrections for potential shared-informant variance, and allow for rigorous cross-respondent prediction.

Further, more data may uncover additional informative domains not found to be prominent in this study, and sensitivity analyses assigning uncertainty to domain contribution estimates would also allow for more definitive indications of what symptom-scales might be missing.

Moreover, pairing these methods with separation of symptom-and functioning-related domains extracted from text may also provide further insight into the nature of unique information in text relevant to impact.
This project also serves as a proof of concept for a framework that has many applications.

With more data, modeling paradigms more complex than regression (such as tree-based methods or neural networks) could capture non-linear feature interactions in both Q and T, increasing understanding of the relationships of factors both within and across these sources.

Different taxonomies and/or combinations of taxonomies could also be explored to find differences between populations (sex, age, culture, etc) at a mass-scale, given the availability of structured and unstructured data across these groups.

Additionally, beyond specifically S, Q, and T, this residual stacking framework may also be applied to any combination of sources, aiding in isolating signal within frameworks previously thought to be inseparable.
Finally, it may also be promising to shift the use of LLMs from deriving a score for each outcome within a taxonomy to exploring the addition of new symptom scale questions.

As opposed to characterizing the nature of relevant information available in various sources of data, this proposed method differs from the framework described in this study in that it allows for the direct and explicit experimentation of potential changes to established screening measures, which may extend beyond the DAWBA.

Allowing for the consideration of both theory and observed results in prior research to develop new structured questionnaire items, this method could leverage existing data to inform real, practical change, without the necessity of conducting new trials.
Depression is common and increasingly prevalent among adolescents, yet it remains less studied in this population than in adults, and is difficult to measure with structured instruments alone.
Free-text descriptions from adolescents and their parents offer a way to capture aspects of the experience that fixed questionnaire items may miss.
In this preregistered study, we tested whether LLM-derived features of free text add predictive signal for depression impact beyond structured symptom-scale items in the DAWBA depression section.
In parent reports, text features explained additional variance in impact beyond item-level symptom ratings, both alone (QT vs.
Q) and combined with sum-scores (SQT vs.
SQ).
This contribution was approximately additive to that of the structured items, suggesting that parent free text carries information about impact that the symptom-scale does not.
These effects were not observed in adolescent self-reports, and text did not outperform item-level symptom ratings as a supplement to sum-scores in either response sample.

Exploratory attribution analyses indicated that the added variance explained by text in these parent-report models was concentrated in functioning-related domains, such as social exclusion, professional responsibilities, and autonomy, rather than in the symptoms the structured symptom-scale items are designed to assess.
Whether this reflects capture of the content that the structured symptom-scale items miss or a finer-grained description of the impairment being predicted remains to be determined.
Given the modest sample and wide uncertainty in effect sizes, these findings should be regarded as preliminary.
More broadly, the residual stacking framework outlined here offers a way to quantify what semi-structured text adds to structured measurement using data that has already been collected.
It can be extended to other taxonomies, populations, informants, and outcomes to test what any one source of data contributes to a given measure beyond the others.

A number of methods and configurations to derive numerical representations of text were explored in the development set, with two main classes: previously trained logistic regression (LR) and LLM prompting.
The goal of both was to represent text as a vector of variables, quantifying the degree of presence in the text of items from a taxonomy of mental health symptoms/outcomes/domains.

text.text: The 31 outcomes were derived from the original 30 by splitting "Other peer relationships" into "Peer relationships" and "Romantic relationships."

We similarly classified the presence of these outcomes for each of monologue (interviewee utterances) and dialogue (interviewer-interviewee) transcription segmentation types, using logistic regression classifiers trained to predict human-coded labels from embeddings of segmentations derived via Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (temperature=0.6).
Due to outcome prevalence imbalances, classifiers were not developed for three of the 31 outcomes.
Logistic regression hyper-parameters (C regularization factor) were derived via 4-fold CV, separately for each segmentation-type/outcome pair.
The set of 56 trained classifiers (one for each of 28 outcomes for each of the two segmentation types) were then available for applying to data derived from the DAWBA.
A number of aggregation methods for the 10 question-answer pairs of DAWBA free-text was also explored: Max, Avg, Block.
For Max and Avg, each of the 10 question-answer pairs were embedded and passed through logistic regression models separately, resulting in 10 feature vectors of length 28.
The maximum and average was then taken over the 10 vectors at each position for Max and Avg, respectively, resulting in a single 28-dimensional feature vector for each.

In the Block method, all 10 question-answer pairs were concatenated to form one large block of text, which was embedded and passed through logistic regression classifiers as a single entity, resulting in a single 28-dimensional feature vector.
Llama 3.3 70B Instruct with temperature of 0.6 was the only configuration utilized for all embeddings of this method.
The class of segmentation type and aggregation method were deemed pseudo-hyperparameters, and their selection is described in further detail in Model Configuration Selection.
The other class of LLM-derived numerical representations involves prompting LLMs about the presence and/or intensity of some taxonomy of mental health outcomes in some input text.

### Task Your task is to analyze the parent's responses to a questionnaire (at most 10 questions) and rate the severity of irritability associated with his/her child, by answering the question below.
The input contains responses from a parent, structured as question/answer pairs (up to Q10/A10).
Each answer is written by the parent and may contain relevant behavioral observations about the child.
---### Instructions -Consider both explicit statements and reasonable implicit indications.
-Base your judgment only on the information provided in the parent's responses.
-Evaluate the responses either collectively or each question independently, as appropriate.
-Use reasonable clinical inference when evidence is indirect or implied.
-Respond with exactly one token from the provided options.
-Do not generate any additional text.
-The output must exactly match one of the provided response options.
---Definition of Irritability: A persistent tendency to react to stimuli with feelings of frustration, annoyance, or anger, often disproportionate to the situation.
It can manifest as a low tolerance for frustration, heightened sensitivity to perceived provocations, and a tendency toward outbursts (verbal or behavioral) that are hard to control.

Irritability may present continuously (a generally short fuse or grumpy baseline mood) or episodically (discrete outbursts triggered by specific events), and can be directed at others (snapping, arguing, aggression) or turned inward (tension, restlessness, frustration).
